headline: Maryland moves over-limit hemp products behind dispensary counters
dek: Maryland told dispensaries on 13 November that hemp products over the new federal 0.4mg THC cap can still be sold from 11 December if they meet state rules.
key_points: The Maryland Cannabis Administration's 13 November bulletin says that from 11 December, hemp products sold in a dispensary's public waiting area must meet the new federal definition of hemp.
Products that fail the federal test can still be sold in the restricted service area, but only if they meet Maryland's cannabis manufacturing, testing, packaging and labelling rules.
Dispensaries that want to send non-compliant stock back to suppliers are told to do it before 11 December.

The guidance gives licensed stores a legal home for products that smoke shops and gas stations will lose, while the FDA has still not published the cannabinoid lists and 'container' definition the federal law depends on.
body: Maryland has told its licensed cannabis dispensaries how to handle the federal hemp cap that takes effect on 11 December, and the answer is to move stronger products behind the counter rather than off the shelf. In a bulletin dated 13 November, the Maryland Cannabis Administration (MCA) said dispensaries that sell hemp-derived products in their public waiting areas should, from 11 December, limit those sales to products that meet the new federal definition of hemp.

Everything else can stay on sale in the restricted service area, the part of the store where regulated cannabis is sold, as long as it meets the MCA's manufacturing, testing, packaging and labelling requirements. The regulator told dispensaries to work with licensed processors to bring non-compliant products up to state standards, and to arrange any returns to suppliers before the deadline.
## What the bulletin says

The MCA bulletin is short and practical. It sets out the federal change, then gives dispensaries three instructions. First, the public waiting area becomes a federal-compliant zone from 11 December: only products that meet the revised definition of hemp and of a final hemp-derived cannabinoid product may be sold there. Second, products that fail the federal test may be sold only in the restricted service area, and only if they satisfy Maryland's own product rules. Third, licensees that plan to return non-compliant products to the businesses that sold them should do so before 11 December.

The regulator also asked dispensaries to review the cannabinoid make-up and paperwork for the hemp products they already hold, warning that some items marketed as hemp may no longer qualify. Questions go to the MCA's compliance and policy inboxes, the bulletin says.
## The federal rule behind it

The change comes from the full-year agriculture spending law Congress passed and President Trump signed on 12 November 2025 (P.L. 119-37). It rewrote the federal definition of hemp in 7 U.S.C. 1639o. Hemp must now contain no more than 0.3% total THC on a dry-weight basis, counting THCA, rather than delta-9 THC alone. The law also excludes three kinds of products from the definition: those with cannabinoids the cannabis plant cannot produce naturally, those with natural cannabinoids synthesised outside the plant, and finished products with more than 0.4 milligrams per container of total THC and similar cannabinoids.

The Congressional Research Service explains that a stopgap funding law passed on 2 September 2026 (P.L. 119-103) split the start date. The ban on cannabinoids the plant cannot produce took effect on 12 November, as we reported that day. The rest, including the 0.4mg container cap, starts on 11 December. Products caught by the exclusions are treated as marijuana under the Controlled Substances Act, CRS says. The law defines a container as the innermost packaging in direct contact with the product.
> Maryland has turned a federal ban into a store-layout rule: the strong hemp products don't vanish, they move to the cannabis side of the counter.
## What changes on Maryland's shop floor

Maryland already split hemp sales inside dispensaries before this bulletin. Under the MCA's dispensary guidance, last updated on 4 September, hemp products with more than 0.5mg of THC per serving or 2.5mg per package could only be sold if they were made, processed and tested under MCA rules, and only in the service area. Products below those levels, plus some full-spectrum tinctures and non-ingestible items such as lotions and pet CBD, could sit in the public zone.

The new bulletin tightens the public zone. A package with 2.5mg of THC, which Maryland's existing threshold allowed in the waiting area, holds more than six times the federal 0.4mg-per-container cap. From 11 December, a product like that would have to move to the service area and meet state cannabis rules, or leave the store. That is MetaFlora's reading of the two documents side by side; the MCA has not published a list of affected products.

The bulletin does not change who may sell intoxicating hemp in Maryland. It gives licensed dispensaries a route to keep selling products that will no longer count as federal hemp, provided those products pass through the state's regulated supply chain. Retailers outside that system, such as smoke shops, get no such route from the MCA bulletin.
## What shops outside the system face

For unlicensed retailers the picture is starker. Reason reported on 14 November from Florida, where small shop owners said hemp products make up about a fifth of their revenue and one St. Petersburg operator told the Florida Phoenix in July that hemp-derived THC made up about 80% of sales at his two stores. The U.S. Hemp Roundtable estimates that roughly 95% of hemp-derived products sold today will become federally illegal under the cap, Reason reported. A single 5mg gummy carries more than 12 times the per-container limit.

States are taking different routes. As we reported on 13 November, Missouri and Illinois have begun enforcing their own 0.4mg caps, pushing stronger products into licensed dispensaries, and New Jersey has extended hemp drink sales to 11 December. Maryland's approach sits in the same family: keep the products inside the licensed market, under cannabis rules.
## The definitions still missing

Compliance is harder because the FDA has not done its part. The 2025 law gave the agency 90 days to publish lists of naturally occurring cannabinoids, THC-class cannabinoids and other cannabinoids with similar effects, and to give more detail on the term 'container'. That deadline was 10 February. Marijuana Moment reported on 9 November that the lists still had not appeared and that the Congressional Research Service had flagged the gap at least three times.

Congress has not moved the 11 December date either. CRS notes that the House-passed FY2027 agriculture spending bill (H.R. 8646) contains no delay, while other bills would push the change back two years (H.R. 7024, H.R. 7010 and S. 3686) or repeal it (H.R. 6209). As we reported this morning, Senators Pete Ricketts and Amy Klobuchar are publicly split on whether to delay further. Reason noted that the Lawful Hemp Protection Act from Reps. Andy Barr and Angie Craig would replace the ban with federal testing, labelling and age rules.
## What to watch

11 December is the date that matters: Maryland's public-area restriction and the federal 0.4mg cap both start then, unless Congress changes the law in its year-end funding bill. Before then, watch for the FDA's cannabinoid lists and container guidance, which would tell dispensaries and processors exactly which products qualify. In Maryland, watch whether processors can reformulate, test and relabel hemp products fast enough for dispensaries to keep them on sale, and whether the MCA issues further guidance on returns. Other states with licensed markets may copy the Maryland model of moving over-limit hemp behind the counter rather than banning it outright.
